records.answer: When L is omitted, repeated calls to the documented f(a, L=[]) accumulate values because the default value for L is evaluated only once, and it is a mutable object (like a list). This means that the same list is reused across function calls, leading to the accumulation of values [doc_e94742212cb6e9b2f35c_p0_c35]. The L=None alternative avoids sharing the default list by checking if L is None and initializing a new list if it is, thus ensuring that each function call has its own separate list [doc_e94742212cb6e9b2f35c_p0_c36].
records.assessment: Supported in the question’s omitted-argument scope. New-list wording should remain conditional on L being omitted or None; an explicitly supplied list can still be shared.

records.answer: The GOV.UK guide does not support the first rule of removing every specialist term even when a user needs it. The guide states that specialist terms can be used if needed, and they should be explained the first time they are used [doc_9f26104ace24902c0800_p0_c3]. The guide also does not support the second rule of rewriting every passive sentence even when the passive wording is more user-centred. The guide acknowledges that passive voice can be appropriate when the outcome is more important than the agent of the action or when the writing is more user-centred [doc_9f26104ace24902c0800_p0_c7]. A revision policy that preserves the guide's general aims and both exceptions could include: use specialist terms when necessary and explain them the first time they are used, and use passive voice when the outcome is more important than the agent of the action or when the writing is more user-centred.
records.assessment: Both exceptions are correctly supported by c3 and c7, but the requested revised policy omits the general plain-English/accessibility aim supported by c0/c1/c2. The general active-voice preference passage c6 was excluded from the reranked context; that retrieval limitation is separate from the omission of available clarity guidance.
